summary: This is the first experimental demonstration of distributed error detection and correction: stabilizers are measured across two trapped-ion modules about 2 m apart, using a photonically generated Bell pair between network qubits as a shared ancilla for the data qubits. A distributed $[[2,1,1]]$ repetition code detects phase flips in real time, and feedforward corrects arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a Bell state shared between the modules.
motivation: Photonic links would let physical qubits be spread over modules and supply the non-local connectivity that high-rate qLDPC codes need. Syndrome extraction between data qubits in different processors had not been shown experimentally.
method: The network Bell pair allows the parity of the two remote data qubits to be read out with only local mixed-species ($^{88}\mathrm{Sr}^+$/$^{43}\mathrm{Ca}^+$) gates and classical communication. Phase-flip errors are injected with probability $p$ through random $Z$ rotations, and depolarizing noise of strength $\lambda$ is applied for the Bell-state test.
result: At zero injected error the stabilizer measurement returns the target outcome with probability 96.4(6)%; conditioning on it keeps the logical qubit in the code space and lowers the logical error over the full range of $p$, and repeating it does not measurably raise the logical error rate. With correction the Bell-state fidelity stays roughly constant against $\lambda$ (the prepared state is 82.5(15)%), limited mainly by the local mixed-species gates, and sympathetic recooling adds 2.2 ms per round, cutting the entanglement rate from about 100/s to 10/s.
